samples.summary: Test titled "does not crash when a callback arrives before anyone awaits it" cannot fail — it never exercises a rejection
samples.evidence: The test hits `/callback?code=unbound` on a server built with the default `allowUnbound: false`. In `login.ts:306-317` that branch writes a 400 and `return`s — it never calls `callbackReject`, and it never settles `callbackPromise`. The test then asserts `settledWithin(waitForCallback(), 50)` is `null`, i.e. that the promise is still pending. The behaviour the test claims to protect is the `callbackPromise.catch(() => {})` guard at login.ts:259, which only matters when the promise REJECTS before anyone awaits it — the only such path is the 30s timeout at login.ts:373-385, which this test never reaches. Deleting login.ts:259 entirely leaves this test green, so it is fake coverage for the unhandled-rejection guard.

samples.summary: The new timeout-message selection (`sawUnboundCallback ? UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE : 'Login timed out…'`) has no test
samples.evidence: login.ts:373-385 introduces a version-skew branch: after a nonce-less callback was seen, the login must fail at the timeout with `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE` rather than the generic timeout text. The comment at login.ts:298-305 presents this as the whole user-facing consequence of refusing an unbound callback. No test in packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts drives the timeout (it is a hard-coded 30_000ms with no injection point and no fake timers used anywhere in the file), so the branch — and the fact that `sawUnboundCallback` is what selects the message — is entirely unexercised; only the constant's use in the 400 response body is asserted (line 100).

samples.summary: The `login` action wiring that keeps the nonce out of argv/stderr is untested; only the primitives it composes are
samples.evidence: The security claim of the change is that `login` prints and `open()`s `startUrl` (nonce-free) while the nonce-carrying URL only ever leaves via the `/start` redirect (login.ts:66-75). The tests cover `buildAuthorizeUrl`, `startUrl` and the `/start` route in isolation, but the only test of the command itself (login-callback.test.ts:226-237) asserts nothing more than that the `--allow-unbound-callback` option is registered. If the action regressed to `console.error(authorizeUrl)` / `open(buildAuthorizeUrl(...))`, or forgot the `setAuthorizeUrl` call, every existing test would still pass. Also untested: `allowUnboundCallback` being threaded into `startCallbackServer`'s `allowUnbound` option (login.ts:48-50).

samples.summary: No test asserts that a nonce-less CLI flow omits `&state=` — the pre-existing regex matches either way
samples.evidence: auth.controller.ts:130-134 adds a conditional: `state.cliState ? '&state=…' : ''`. The new test (spec:218-235) covers the truthy branch. The falsy branch is only touched by the older test at spec:189-212, whose matcher is `/^http:\/\/127\.0\.0\.1:9876\/callback\?code=.+/` — unanchored at the end, so it passes whether or not a `&state=` (or a stale/undefined one, e.g. `&state=undefined`) is appended. Nothing fails if the else-branch regresses.

samples.summary: `encodeURIComponent(state.cliState)` on the echoed nonce is never exercised with a value that needs encoding
samples.evidence: The only nonce used in the new controller test is `'nonce-abc'` (spec:221), which encodes to itself; removing `encodeURIComponent` at auth.controller.ts:131 leaves the suite green. A nonce containing `&`, `=` or `#` (the CLI mints base64url so it is safe in practice, but the guard's `CLI_STATE_PATTERN` allows `-`/`_` only after validation, and the store accepts any string) would split the redirect query undetected.

samples.summary: "prints the GET without fetching or writing the file" never asserts that no file was written
samples.evidence: The test name promises the export dry run does not write `out.csv`, but the body only asserts `getCells` was not called and checks stdout JSON. `writeFileSync` (sheets-export.ts:71) is neither spied nor mocked, and no fs assertion exists, so the write half of the claim is uncovered. (In practice the write is unreachable once the fetch is skipped, but the test as written proves nothing about it, and a mis-placed dry-run branch that fell through to the writer with empty data would still pass the stdout assertion only by luck.)

samples.summary: The new `--range` query mirroring in the sheets-export dry run is untested
samples.evidence: sheets-export.ts:48-55 adds range encoding duplicated from `HttpClient.getCells`, which is exactly the kind of copy that can drift. read-dry-run.test.ts:181-190 only runs `sheets export doc-1 out.csv --dry-run` with no `--range`, so the `?range=…` branch (and its `encodeURIComponent`) has no coverage; the analogous branch for `cells get` is covered at line 168 but that is a different code path.

samples.summary: `files list` ordering of `--type` validation before the dry-run branch has no test, unlike the identical `docs list` case
samples.evidence: files.ts:81-93 adds the same 'validate BEFORE preview' ordering that docs.ts:75 does, and read-dry-run.test.ts:121-129 tests it for `docs list --type slides --dry-run`. No equivalent case exists for `files list --type bogus --dry-run` (the parameterised `%s list/get` block at read-dry-run.test.ts:202-228 exercises only the plain list/get), so reordering the files.ts branches would go unnoticed.

samples.summary: Weakened fail-safe test: `assert.equal(out.full, true)` no longer demonstrates the empty-string fall-through
samples.evidence: The env now includes `GITHUB_EVENT_NAME: 'push', GITHUB_REF_NAME: 'main'`, which changed-areas.mjs:530-532 short-circuits to FULL regardless of the `WAFFLEBASE_CHANGED_AREAS` handling the test is named for. `out.full === true` is therefore true even if the empty-string branch regressed to something benign. Only the new `assert.match(out.reasons.join(' '), /push to main/)` still discriminates (a regression that consumed the empty string would report a different reason). The primary assertion is now decorative; the discriminating one should carry the test's intent explicitly.

samples.summary: Over-mocking: the whole `HttpClient` is replaced, so the file's central claim ("the preview is the request") is checked against hardcoded literals, not against the real builder
samples.evidence: `vi.mock('../src/client/http-client.js')` stubs the entire client, so every expected preview URL in this file is a string literal written by hand. If `HttpClient.base`/`apiKeysUrl` changed shape, these tests would still pass while the preview and the real request diverged — which is precisely the drift the diff's comments (api-keys.ts:9-14, dry-run.ts:22-26) say the shared builder prevents. url.test.ts and http-client-paths.test.ts each pin one side, but nothing asserts the two agree.

samples.summary: `expect(guard.canActivate(context)).toBe(true)` asserts the mocked super-class return value, not guard behaviour
samples.evidence: `AuthGuard('github').prototype.canActivate` is stubbed to `true` in beforeEach (spec:44-56), so the `toBe(true)` assertions in the three positive cases hold no matter what the guard does with `cliState`. The meaningful assertions in those tests are the `createState` / `consumeState` ones; the `toBe(true)` line is inert and could mislead a later reader into thinking the passport leg is covered.

finding.summary: Test titled "does not crash when a callback arrives before anyone awaits it" cannot fail — it never exercises a rejection
finding.evidence: The test hits `/callback?code=unbound` on a server built with the default `allowUnbound: false`. In `login.ts:306-317` that branch writes a 400 and `return`s — it never calls `callbackReject`, and it never settles `callbackPromise`. The test then asserts `settledWithin(waitForCallback(), 50)` is `null`, i.e. that the promise is still pending. The behaviour the test claims to protect is the `callbackPromise.catch(() => {})` guard at login.ts:259, which only matters when the promise REJECTS before anyone awaits it — the only such path is the 30s timeout at login.ts:373-385, which this test never reaches. Deleting login.ts:259 entirely leaves this test green, so it is fake coverage for the unhandled-rejection guard.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repo. The test at login-callback.test.ts:121-134 hits `/callback?code=unbound` on a server created with default options (line 125, no `allowUnbound`), which lands in login.ts:306-317 — that branch writes 400, warns, and `return`s without ever calling `callbackReject`, leaving `callbackPromise` pending. The behavior the test's title/comment claims to protect is the pre-attached `callbackPromise.catch(() => {})` at login.ts:259, whose only triggering path is the 30 s timeout rejection at login.ts:373-385; the test never advances that timer (no fake timers in the file) and `srv.close()` at line 132 clears the timeout via login.ts:404-407. So no rejection is ever produced and deleting login.ts:259 would leave the test green — it is fake coverage for the unhandled-rejection guard, and its only real assertions duplicate the earlier test at lines 98-105. Grep confirms `startCallbackServer`/`waitForCallback` appear in no other test file, so nothing else covers the rejection-before-await path. The reviewer's "cannot fail" wording is slightly overstated (the `toBeNull()` assertion would fail if the unbound branch rejected), but the substantive claim — the test never exercises a rejection and gives no coverage for the guard it is named after — holds, which is major under the test-adequacy rubric.

finding.summary: The new timeout-message selection (`sawUnboundCallback ? UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE : 'Login timed out…'`) has no test
finding.evidence: login.ts:373-385 introduces a version-skew branch: after a nonce-less callback was seen, the login must fail at the timeout with `UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE` rather than the generic timeout text. The comment at login.ts:298-305 presents this as the whole user-facing consequence of refusing an unbound callback. No test in packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts drives the timeout (it is a hard-coded 30_000ms with no injection point and no fake timers used anywhere in the file), so the branch — and the fact that `sawUnboundCallback` is what selects the message — is entirely unexercised; only the constant's use in the 400 response body is asserted (line 100).

verdict.reason: The claim holds. startCallbackServer rejects at a hard-coded setTimeout(..., 30_000) (login.ts:373-385) with the message chosen by `sawUnboundCallback ? UNBOUND_CALLBACK_MESSAGE : 'Login timed out...'`, and the options bag (login.ts:232-234) exposes no timeout/clock injection point. Repo-wide search found exactly one importer of startCallbackServer (packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:9); the literal 'Login timed out' appears only at login.ts:380 and docs/design/cli.md:193; no CLI test uses fake timers (useFakeTimers/advanceTimersByTime occur only in packages/slides/test/view/present/presenter.test.ts and packages/backend/test/http.e2e-spec.ts). Moreover every test in login-callback.test.ts closes the server in a finally block, and close() calls clearTimeout(timeout) (login.ts:404-407), so the timer is cancelled before it can ever fire. The unbound-callback test (lines 92-119) only asserts the 400 body, the single warning, non-settlement within 50ms, and that a later valid callback wins — it never asserts which error the login ultimately fails with. The code comment at login.ts:298-305 presents the version-skew message at the timeout as the user-facing consequence of refusing an unbound callback, so this is a real behavior shipped with no meaningful test: major missing-test under the test-adequacy rubric. No counterexample exists anywhere in the tree.

finding.summary: Test 'does not crash when a callback arrives before anyone awaits it' cannot fail — the path it claims to cover no longer rejects
finding.evidence: The test drives `/callback?code=unbound` and asserts a 400 plus that the promise has not settled. But after this delta the nonce-less branch (src/commands/login.ts:306-317) never calls `callbackReject` — it only warns and returns. The only remaining rejection path is the 30s timeout, which the test never reaches. So the guard the test exists to protect (`callbackPromise.catch(() => {})`, login.ts:259) could be deleted entirely and this test would still pass; it is now an exact duplicate of the assertions in the preceding test at line 92. To be meaningful it would have to trigger an actual pre-await rejection (e.g. an injectable/faked timeout) and assert no unhandled rejection occurred.

verdict.reason: Verified directly. The nonce-less callback branch (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:306-317) writes 400, warns once, and returns — it never calls callbackReject. The only callbackReject site is the 30s timeout (login.ts:373-385), which the test at packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts:121-134 never reaches: it waits only 50ms via settledWithin and its finally-block calls srv.close(), which clears the timeout (login.ts:404-407). So the promise is never rejected during that test, and the guard the test claims to protect (callbackPromise.catch(() => {}), login.ts:259) could be deleted with both assertions (status 400, settledWithin === null) still passing — the test cannot fail on the behavior stated in its own comment (lines 122-124). Its assertions are also a strict subset of the preceding test (lines 98-105), which drives the identical /callback?code=unbound request. No test in the file injects or fakes a pre-await rejection, so the guard at login.ts:259 has no meaningful coverage. Vacuous test presented as coverage = major under the test-adequacy rubric.

finding.summary: No test covers login.ts's actual hand-off: that `open()` and stderr receive `startUrl` and not the nonce-bearing URL

It never touches the login action handler, so the security property it names — login.ts:66-72 printing `startUrl` and passing `startUrl` (not `buildAuthorizeUrl(...)`) to `open()` — is untested: swapping line 67 or line 72 back to the nonce-carrying URL would break the stated guarantee with every test still green. The only test of the action-registering function (test line 226) asserts merely that the command and the `--allow-unbound-callback` option exist, which says nothing about the hand-off.

verdict.reason: The login action's hand-off is genuinely untested. login.ts:66-72 prints and passes `startUrl` (not the nonce-carrying authorize URL) to `console.error` and `open()`, which is the security property the change advertises. The test titled "keeps the nonce out of the URL handed to the browser and to stderr" (login-callback.test.ts:184-206) constructs its own `startCallbackServer`, calls `setAuthorizeUrl` itself, and asserts only on the returned `startUrl` string and the `/start` 302 — it never invokes the command action, never captures stderr, and never observes `open`. The only `registerLoginCommand` test (login-callback.test.ts:227-236) asserts only that the command and `--allow-unbound-callback` option exist. I searched wide for a counterexample: repo-wide grep for `startUrl`/`setAuthorizeUrl` outside node_modules yields only login.ts and that one test file; grep for `Opening browser` yields only login.ts; grep for `'open'` across packages/**/*.ts finds no mock/spy of the `open` module (only a prose comment at login-callback.test.ts:122-124); grep for `registerLoginCommand`/`commands/login` finds only that test, cli.ts and docs; `packages/backend/test/**` has no login e2e; no `parseAsync` call site anywhere drives the login command. Swapping line 67 or 72 back to `buildAuthorizeUrl(...)` would leave every test green.
